values.label: Ventricular muscle fiber, resting membrane potential
values.where: Chapter 10, Rhythmical Excitation of the Heart: 'Mechanism of Sinus Nodal Rhythmicity', where the sinus nodal fiber is compared with the ventricular muscle fiber (-85 to -90 millivolts).
values.note: The teaching model does not change this value: none of the drug classes here acts mainly on the resting potential.

values.label: Ventricular action potential, peak
values.where: Chapter 9, Cardiac Muscle; The Heart as a Pump and Function of the Heart Valves: 'Action Potentials in Cardiac Muscle' (the potential rises to a slightly positive value, about +20 millivolts, each beat).
values.note: The source gives a single approximate value, not a range.

values.label: Ventricular action potential, plateau duration
values.where: Chapter 9: 'Action Potentials in Cardiac Muscle' (after the initial spike the membrane remains depolarized for about 0.2 second, exhibiting a plateau).
values.note: The source gives a single approximate value, not a range.

values.label: Ventricular refractory period
values.where: Chapter 9: 'Refractory Period of Cardiac Muscle' (the normal refractory period of the ventricle is 0.25 to 0.30 second).
values.note: The model takes the refractory period to end when the voltage has fallen most of the way back to rest.

values.label: Sinus nodal fiber, most negative potential between beats
values.where: Chapter 10: 'Mechanism of Sinus Nodal Rhythmicity' (between discharges the sinus nodal fiber has a maximum negativity of about -55 to -60 millivolts).

values.label: Sinus nodal fiber, threshold for discharge
values.where: Chapter 10: 'Mechanism of Sinus Nodal Rhythmicity' (when the potential reaches a threshold voltage of about -40 millivolts, the action potential begins).
values.note: The teaching model keeps the threshold fixed; drugs and nerves move the drift toward it instead.

values.label: Sinus node, rhythmical discharge rate
values.where: Chapter 10: 'Sinus Node as the Pacemaker of the Heart' (the normal rate of the sinus node is 70 to 80 times per minute, against 40 to 60 for the A-V nodal fibers and 15 to 40 for the Purkinje fibers).

values.label: QRS complex duration (electrocardiogram)
values.where: Chapter 12, Electrocardiographic Interpretation of Cardiac Muscle and Coronary Blood Flow Abnormalities: Vectorial Analysis: 'Prolonged and Bizarre Patterns of the QRS Complex' (the normal QRS complex lasts 0.06 to 0.08 second, as long as depolarization is still spreading through the ventricles).
values.note: The model treats the QRS duration as the time the signal takes to spread through the ventricles, so it lengthens as the muscle cells' upswing slows.

values.label: Q-T interval (electrocardiogram)
values.where: Chapter 11, The Normal Electrocardiogram: 'Q-T Interval' (from the beginning of the Q wave to the end of the T wave; ordinarily about 0.35 second).
values.note: The source gives a single approximate value, not a range. The model scales it with the plateau and fall of the ventricular action potential.

states.label: Sympathetic stimulation
states.summary: Noradrenaline from sympathetic nerves makes the pacemaker cells' membranes more permeable to sodium and calcium, so their voltage between beats sits higher and drifts up to threshold faster, and the sinus node fires more often.
states.where: Chapter 10, 'Control of Heart Rhythmicity and Impulse Conduction by the Cardiac Nerves': 'Mechanism of the Sympathetic Effect'.

states.label: Parasympathetic (vagal) stimulation
states.summary: Acetylcholine from the vagus nerves makes the pacemaker cells' membranes more permeable to potassium, so their voltage between beats falls further below threshold and the sinus node fires less often.
states.where: Chapter 10, 'Control of Heart Rhythmicity and Impulse Conduction by the Cardiac Nerves': 'Mechanism of the Vagal Effects' (the sinus nodal fibers are hyperpolarized to -65 to -75 millivolts).

states.label: Sodium channel blockers, class IA
states.summary: They block the fast sodium channels that make the heart muscle cell's rapid upswing; class IA drugs widen the QRS complex and lengthen the Q-T interval.
states.where: Section 2.2.1 Vaughan Williams Classification and Table 5: "Class IA drugs prolong the PR interval, QRS duration, and QT interval, class IB drugs shorten the QT interval without effects on the PR interval nor QRS duration, and class IC drugs prolong the PR interval and QRS duration without effects on the QT interval".
states.mechanismWhere: Chapter 9: 'Action Potentials in Cardiac Muscle' (the rapid upstroke spike is caused by opening of the fast sodium channels), the channel these drugs block.
states.modelNote: The model shows class IA as a moderate sodium block that slows the upswing and the spread, plus a partial potassium block that lengthens the plateau.

states.label: Sodium channel blockers, class IB
states.summary: They block the fast sodium channels that make the heart muscle cell's rapid upswing, but let go quickly; class IB drugs shorten the Q-T interval and leave the QRS duration unchanged.
states.where: Section 2.2.1 Vaughan Williams Classification and Table 5: "Class IA drugs prolong the PR interval, QRS duration, and QT interval, class IB drugs shorten the QT interval without effects on the PR interval nor QRS duration, and class IC drugs prolong the PR interval and QRS duration without effects on the QT interval".
states.mechanismWhere: Chapter 9: 'Action Potentials in Cardiac Muscle' (the rapid upstroke spike is caused by opening of the fast sodium channels), the channel these drugs block.
states.modelNote: The model shows class IB as a very light sodium block at a normal heart rate, so the upswing and spread barely change, plus a slightly shorter plateau.

states.label: Sodium channel blockers, class IC
states.summary: They strongly block the fast sodium channels that make the heart muscle cell's rapid upswing; class IC drugs widen the QRS complex and leave the Q-T interval unchanged.
states.where: Section 2.2.1 Vaughan Williams Classification and Table 5: "Class IA drugs prolong the PR interval, QRS duration, and QT interval, class IB drugs shorten the QT interval without effects on the PR interval nor QRS duration, and class IC drugs prolong the PR interval and QRS duration without effects on the QT interval".
states.mechanismWhere: Chapter 9: 'Action Potentials in Cardiac Muscle' (the rapid upstroke spike is caused by opening of the fast sodium channels), the channel these drugs block.
states.modelNote: The model shows class IC as a strong sodium block: a slower, lower upswing and slower spread, with the plateau and fall untouched.

states.label: Beta-blockers (class II)
states.summary: They block the beta receptors through which noradrenaline makes the pacemaker cells drift toward threshold faster, so the heart slows.
states.where: Table 4, medications that can induce bradycardia or conduction disorders: beta-adrenergic receptor blockers are listed.
states.mechanismWhere: Chapter 10, 'Control of Heart Rhythmicity and Impulse Conduction by the Cardiac Nerves': 'Mechanism of the Sympathetic Effect' (noradrenaline raises the pacemaker membrane's permeability to sodium and calcium, speeding the drift to threshold).
states.modelNote: The cited table describes slowing of the heart only.

states.label: Potassium channel blockers (class III)
states.summary: They block potassium channels, and potassium leaving the cell is what ends the heart muscle cell's plateau, so the action potential, the refractory period and the Q-T interval lengthen.
states.where: Section 2.2.1 Vaughan Williams Classification: "class III agents prolonging action potential duration (APD)" and "APD prolongation by class III drugs is caused by K+ channel blockade"; Table 5: "Class III APD prolongation (K+ channel blockade) amiodarone, sotalol, nifekalant" (plateau duration up). Table 61, Causes of Acquired Long QT Syndrome: "Class III (sotalol, nifekalant, amiodarone, etc.)" (Q-T interval up). Figure 3D (mechanism of reentry): "Drugs that prolong refractory period, such as class III drugs" (refractory period up).
states.mechanismWhere: Chapter 9: 'Action Potentials in Cardiac Muscle' (at the end of the plateau, potassium permeability rises rapidly and the loss of potassium returns the membrane to its resting level), the process these drugs slow.
states.modelNote: The guideline speaks of action potential duration; the plateau is most of it, so the model lengthens the plateau and the fall.

states.label: Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (class IV)
states.summary: They block the L-type calcium channels whose opening at threshold makes the pacemaker cells' upswing, so the sinus node fires more slowly.
states.where: Table 4, medications that can induce bradycardia or conduction disorders: nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are listed.
states.mechanismWhere: Chapter 10: 'Mechanism of Sinus Nodal Rhythmicity' (when the pacemaker voltage reaches threshold, L-type calcium channels activate and cause the action potential).
states.modelNote: The cited table describes slowing of the heart only. In the model the muscle cell's plateau also sits a little lower.
